summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: F.K. v. Iowa District Court for Polk County
key_cases.holding: Iowa Code section 232.78, which permits ex parte temporary removal orders on an application that need not be sworn or written, violates neither the Fourth Amendment nor the Warrant Clause nor federal or state due process, because the removal is limited in duration and a reasonably prompt post-removal hearing follows.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Iowa decision on the constitutionality of emergency protective custody under Iowa Code section 232.78, including the ten-day maximum for an ex parte removal.
key_cases.quote: On balance, we cannot say that the protections in place in section 232.78 deprive litigants, such as Felicia, of due process.

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Des Moines detectives conducting a child welfare check were not entitled to qualified immunity for arresting a mother on her porch after she refused their demands: without a warrant, an exigency, a removal order, or her consent, they could neither enter the home nor compel her to produce the child.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that taking protective custody requires a warrant, court order, consent, or a genuine exigency — the four lawful doors.
key_cases.quote: they could not lawfully enter the home without Webster's consent, nor force her to take any specific action with respect to L.B.

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on a motion to dismiss where a child-abuse investigator was alleged to have ordered seven children removed from their home despite contrary evidence and staff recommendations; reasonable suspicion of child abuse is required and is judged on the totality of the circumstances at the time of removal.
key_cases.relevance: States the substantive standard — reasonable suspicion of child abuse on the totality of the circumstances — that must exist when protective custody is taken.
key_cases.quote: whether there was reasonable suspicion of child abuse warranting removal must be determined by analyzing the totality of the circumstances at the time of the removal

key_cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed injunctive relief and the district court's conclusion that a juvenile officer's mass removal of children from a residential school violated the Fourth Amendment — the ex parte orders were tainted by the manner in which they were obtained, and thirty-five children were taken with no court order, probable cause, or exigent circumstances.
key_cases.relevance: The Eighth Circuit's clearest condemnation of mass protective custody taken without individualized court authorization or exigency.
key_cases.quote: upon de novo review, we see no error in the legal conclusions on the reasonableness of the seizures and the Fourth Amendment violation

state_agency.name: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, Child Protective Services

mandatory_reporters: Health practitioners who examine, attend, or treat a child — § 232.69(1)(a)
Employees/operators of public or private health care facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(2)
Licensed school employees, certified para-educators, coaching-authorization holders, school employees age 18 or older, and community college instructors — § 232.69(1)(b)(4)

Employees/operators of licensed child care centers, registered child development homes, head start programs, family development and self-sufficiency grant programs, and HOPES–Healthy Families Iowa programs — § 232.69(1)(b)(5)
Employees/operators of licensed substance use disorder programs or facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(6)
Employees of department institutions listed in Iowa Code § 218.1 — § 232.69(1)(b)(7)
Employees/operators of juvenile detention or juvenile shelter care facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(8)
Employees/operators of child foster care facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(9)
Employees/operators of providers of services to children funded under a federally approved medical assistance home and community-based services waiver — § 232.69(1)(b)(13)
Employees, operators, owners, and others who perform duties for certified children's residential facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(14)
reporting_details: Iowa is a designated-professional reporting state: the classes of persons listed in Iowa Code § 232.69(1) must report suspected child abuse within 24 hours, while any other person may report but is not required to (Iowa Code § 232.69(2)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours (child abuse assessment) or 72 hours (family assessment)
20 business days (child abuse assessment); 10 business days (family assessment)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the child abuse report

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Oral notice to the court of an emergency removal without a court order
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Emergency removal or keeping of the child without a court order

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Written notice to the court of an emergency removal without a court order
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Orally informing the court of the emergency removal under Iowa Code § 232.79(2)(d)

notice_requirements.timing: Within 5 working days of commencing the assessment (Iowa Code § 232.71B(2)); a court may direct the department to withhold notification if it would endanger the child or other persons
